title: Sharp-angle competitive notes: LLM API positioning
body:
Purpose and intended use:
This is a compact, tactical reference for SDRs/AE/solutions engineers to use when debating major LLM API providers on performance, economics, and enterprise risk. Not a comprehensive whitepaper — think: quick hits, pressure points, suggested rebuttals, and demo checks that close deals faster.

One-line positioning to use in first 30s:
- "Redwood is the inference platform that makes your LLM features predictable and inexpensive at scale — same API and controls across hosted, reserved, or fully private deployments, with built-in fallbacks so your product never silently degrades."

Target buyer personas (who to angle at):
- Platform/AI Infra lead: cares about cost predictability, quotas, multi-tenant isolation and observability.
- Product engineering manager: cares about latency, reliability, and dev ergonomics (SDKs, streaming, function calling).
- Security/compliance lead: cares about VPC/private mode, KMS/HSM, audit logs, and legal terms.

Competitive landscape (high level categories):
- Large hyperscaler LLM APIs (monolithic hosted endpoints) — strong model breadth and marketing; weaker on predictable unit economics and private deployments.
- Pure-play LLM API startups — very simple UX, but often single deployment mode (hosted), limited enterprise controls, and brittle fallbacks.
- Self-hosted inference stacks / infra vendors — great for control and cost at very large scale but require heavy ops and engineering lift.

Key customer value dimensions (how buyers judge vendors):
1) Latency tail and SLA guarantees
2) Unit cost predictability and control (batching, caching, quantization guidance)
3) Deployment flexibility: hosted / dedicated / private
4) Observability and debug tools (token-level cost traces, per-route dashboards)
5) Reliability / graceful degradation (fallback policies, region routing)
6) Security & compliance features
7) Developer ergonomics (SDKs, streaming, function/tool calling)

Short competitor map (what we typically hear in calls):
- HyperscalerX: "cheaper at baseline, trusted infra". Pressure: large TCO surprise when scaling, weaker model rollout tools, limited local KV caching.
- CloudStart: "super-simple API, friendly pricing". Pressure: single-tenant noisy neighbors, no private VPC option, basic observability.
- InfraBox (self-hosted): "You run it, you control everything". Pressure: weeks-months of infra work, lost product dev velocity, no managed fallbacks.

Differentiation talking points (lines that close):
- Unified runtime: "You get the exact same API and rollout semantics whether you use our hosted tier, reserve dedicated capacity, or deploy into your VPC — no refactor when you scale or need compliance."
- Cost levers exposed to engineers: "We give actionable knobs (batching configs, KV prefix caching, quantization profiles) + continuous suggestions based on workload so you reduce unit cost without blind quality loss."
- Production safety: "Automatic fallbacks and routing policies keep apps live when a model variant or region is down; we also ship observability to quickly detect regressions."
- Enterprise-ready private deployments: "Customer-managed control plane and KMS integration. You can run air-gapped and maintain auditability required for regulated customers."

Common objections and suggested rebuttals (scripted):
1) "Hyperscaler is cheaper / we already have a contract."
- Rebuttal: "At small volumes that can be true. Where teams get surprised is when latency tails or concurrency requires larger clusters — we’ve seen total per-token and infra costs drift up 20–60% without caching/batching. Redwood’s dedicated and optimizer tooling gives predictable unit economics and automatic mitigation when patterns change."
2) "We can self-host and save money."
- Rebuttal: "If you have a 10+ person infra effort and months to dedicate, that can pay back. For most product teams the opportunity cost is the new features you won’t ship. Redwood’s private offering gives the control of self-host with ~80% less ops overhead and our playbooks for performance tuning."
3) "Your platform is too opinionated / we want raw GPU access."
- Rebuttal: "Our opinionated defaults (batching, cache TTLs, quant profiles) are tunable — they’re informed by thousands of production requests. You can still surface low-level knobs via our console/SDK when needed."
4) "Does caching/quantization break quality?"
- Rebuttal: "We run per-customer evals and provide rollback+ab test hooks; optimizer suggestions come with expected quality impact and a quick eval scaffold so you never apply changes blind."

'Pressure points' (sales traps to push on; items where rivals are commonly weak):
- Lack of multi-mode deployment: ask how the vendor will handle data residency or FedRamp customer requirements.
- Observability limits: ask for token-level cost traces and per-route error breakdowns — many competitors provide only coarse metrics.
- Fallback strategy: ask them to walk through an outage scenario where model variant is exhausted; most hosted vendors only have rate limits and backoff, not model-variant fallbacks.
- Hidden TCO: ask for a detailed example when QPS grows to 10k and vendor needs to scale GPU clusters. Ask for token-level bill breakdown during high concurrency.

Demo checklist for AE/Solutions engineer (what to show live):
1) Quick two-minute setup: show how the same request runs on hosted, dedicated, and private with identical SDK.
2) Console: per-route dashboards, token-cost traces, and latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99).
3) Rollouts: create a canary, show automated rollback on metric regression.
4) Fault demo: simulate model variant exhaustion and show automatic fallback to compatible variant without user-visible error.
5) Optimizer: apply a batching suggestion and show estimated cost delta + a small quality check.
6) Security: walkthrough VPC/private deploy options, KMS key binding, and audit log sample.

Negotiation levers and contract points to highlight for sales ops:
- Commit tiers vs spot/burst capacity: customers often want predictable SLA for peaks; offer tiered reserved vs burst pricing.
- Observability add-ons: longer retention/windowed traces for enterprise at modest additional fee.
- Professional services package: benchmark + migration sprint for customers coming from self-hosted stacks.

Red-team Qs to be prepared for (hard technical follow-ups):
- Show how KV prefix caching works at runtime and how it affects cold-start p99 latency.
- Demonstrate how quantized variants affect logits/temperature behavior for a critical prompt.
- Show a real log sample tracing token-level cost across a conversation that includes streaming and tool calls.

Quick sample rebuttal snippets for Slack/email templates (short):
- "On cost: happy to run a 2-week pilot and show end-to-end token bill and architecture recommendations — most teams see immediate 15–30% savings once prefix caching and batching are applied."
- "On reliability: we can run a simulated outage during the POC to demonstrate our fallback behavior — book a 45-minute session and we’ll show it live."

Open questions for product/engineering (internal follow-ups):
- Can we document a standard demo dataset for showing quantization/quality tradeoffs? (work with applied-ml)
- Collect three recent customer examples where fallback routing prevented a live outage (SRE/customer-success).
- Add a short how-to in console for turning on token-level traces per-route without high retention costs (observability team).

TL;DR (what to memorize):
- Lead with predictable unit economics + deployment flexibility.
- Push competitors on observability and fallback behavior.
- Use demo checklist to show identical API across deployment modes and live fallback.

Notes to self / friction items we fix later:
- Add 1–pager on explainability of optimizer suggestions (why we choose a particular quant profile).
- Make a short video demo for sales to reuse showing a canary rollback.

References / breadcrumbs: link to longer comparisons, internal benchmarks, and PRs in linked_artifacts above.

End of doc — working draft, feel free to copy snippets into battlecards or email templates.
